metadata.title: A Theory of the Learnable
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF→text fallback; .tex source not available. Math fidelity reduced.
metadata.registry_mismatch_note: PDF matches metadata: Valiant 1984, 'A Theory of the Learnable'.

nodes.name: Vector and total vector
nodes.statement: A vector is an assignment to each of the $t$ Boolean variables $p_1, \ldots, p_t$ of a value from $\{0, 1, *\}$, where $*$ denotes undetermined. A vector is total if every variable is determined (i.e., assigned a value from $\{0,1\}$).
nodes.statement_clean: A vector assigns each variable a value in {0,1,*}; it is total when no variable is *.

nodes.name: Boolean function and concept
nodes.statement: A Boolean function $F$ is a mapping from the set of $2^t$ total vectors to $\{0,1\}$. $F$ becomes a concept when its domain is extended to all vectors by setting $F(v)=1$ iff $F(w)=1$ for all total vectors $w$ that agree with $v$ on its determined variables.
nodes.statement_clean: A concept extends a Boolean function to partial vectors: F(v)=1 iff F is true on every total completion of v.

nodes.name: Distribution $D$ on positive examples
nodes.statement: Given a concept $F$, $D$ is an arbitrary probability distribution over $\{v : F(v)=1\}$ with $D(v) \geq 0$ and $\sum D(v) = 1$. $D$ describes the relative frequency with which positive examples occur in nature.

nodes.name: Learning protocol (EXAMPLES, ORACLE)
nodes.statement: The learning protocol provides two routines: EXAMPLES outputs a positive example $v$ with $F(v)=1$ drawn according to $D$; ORACLE($v$) outputs $1$ if $F(v)=1$ and $0$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_clean: The learner has access to a sampler EXAMPLES of positive examples and a membership oracle ORACLE.

nodes.name: Learnability of a class $X$ of programs
nodes.statement: A class $X$ is learnable if there exists an algorithm $A$ (the deduction procedure) using the protocol such that: (1) $A$ runs in time polynomial in $h$, the program size, and the number of variables $t$; (2) for every $f \in X$ and every distribution $D$ on $\{v : f(v)=1\}$, with probability $\geq 1-h^{-1}$, $A$ outputs $g \in X$ with $g(v)=1 \Rightarrow f(v)=1$ and $\sum_{v: f(v)=1, g(v)\neq 1} D(v) \leq h^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_clean: X is learnable if a polynomial-time algorithm produces, with high probability, a one-sided-error approximation g of any target f \in X.

nodes.name: Function $L(h,S)$
nodes.statement: For $h>1$ real and $S \geq 1$ integer, $L(h,S)$ is the smallest integer such that in $L(h,S)$ independent Bernoulli trials each of success probability $\geq h^{-1}$, the probability of fewer than $S$ successes is less than $h^{-1}$.

nodes.name: k-CNF expression
nodes.statement: A CNF expression is a product $c_1 c_2 \cdots c_r$ where each clause $c_i$ is a disjunction of literals (a literal is a variable or its negation). A $k$-CNF expression has every clause of length at most $k$.

nodes.name: DNF expression and prime implicant
nodes.statement: A DNF expression is a sum $m_1 + m_2 + \cdots + m_r$ of monomials (products of literals). A monomial $m$ is a prime implicant of $F$ if $m \Rightarrow F$ but no $m'$ obtained by deleting a literal from $m$ satisfies $m' \Rightarrow F$.

nodes.name: Monotone expression and degree of DNF
nodes.statement: An expression is monotone if no variable is negated. The degree of a DNF expression is the largest number of monomials in any equivalent prime DNF expression. In the monotone case the prime DNF (the sum of all prime implicants) is unique.

nodes.name: $\mu$-expression
nodes.statement: A general expression over $\{p_1,\ldots,p_t\}$ is built recursively from literals via plus and times constructors. A $\mu$-expression is one in which each variable appears at most once; without loss of generality it is monotone and the constructors alternate.

nodes.name: Oracles N-ORACLE, P-ORACLE, PI, RP, RA
nodes.statement: $N$-ORACLE$(v)=1$ iff $F(w)=1$ for all total $w$ extending $v$. $P$-ORACLE$(v)=1$ iff some such total $w$ has $F(w)=1$. $PI(v)=1$ iff $N$-ORACLE$(v)=1$ but flipping any determined variable to $*$ falsifies it. $RP(m)=1$ iff $mm'$ is a prime implicant of $f$ for some monomial $m'$. $RA(V,W)=1$ iff every prime implicant of $f$ touching $V$ also touches $W$.
nodes.statement_clean: Five oracles of increasing power used by the mu-expression learner.

nodes.name: Linear upper bound on $L(h,S)$
nodes.statement: For all integers $S \geq 1$ and all real $h > 1$: $L(h,S) \leq 2h(S + \log_e h)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition (bound on $L(h,S)$)
nodes.statement: Apply Chernoff's tail bound on $m$ Bernoulli trials with success probability $p$: $P[\#\text{successes} \leq k] \leq \binom{m}{k} p^k (1-p)^{m-k}$ rewritten via the inequalities $(1+x^{-1})^x < e$ and $(1-x^{-1})^x < e^{-1}$. Substituting $m = 2h(S+\log h)$, $p = h^{-1}$, $k = S$ yields a bound $\leq h^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Theorem A: $k$-CNF is learnable
nodes.statement: For any positive integer $k$, the class of $k$-CNF expressions is learnable via an algorithm $A$ that uses $L = L(h,(2t)^{k+1})$ calls of EXAMPLES and no calls of ORACLE, where $t$ is the number of variables.
assumptions: target $f$ is a $k$-CNF expression in $t$ variables
conclusions: $f$ is learnable using $L(h,(2t)^{k+1})$ calls of EXAMPLES and no ORACLE calls

nodes.name: Algorithm A: Learn $k$-CNF from positive examples
nodes.statement: Initialize $g$ as the product of all clauses of up to $k$ literals; for each of $L$ positive examples $v$ from EXAMPLES, delete every clause of $g$ not satisfied by $v$.
input: Access to EXAMPLES sampling positive examples of target $f$
output: A $k$-CNF expression $g$ such that $g \Rightarrow f$ and $g$ approximates $f$ within probability $h^{-1}$
nodes.pseudocode: g := product of all clauses with ≤ k literals over {p_i, ¬p_i}; repeat L = L(h, (2t)^{k+1}) times: v := EXAMPLES; for each clause c_i in g: if v ⊭ c_i then delete c_i; return g.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem A
nodes.statement: Show that the maximal $k$-CNF $B$ equivalent to $f$ never has its clauses deleted, so $\{v : v \Rightarrow g\} \subseteq \{v : v \Rightarrow f\}$. The probability that $X = \sum_{v \Rightarrow f, v \not\Rightarrow g} D(v)$ stays $\geq h^{-1}$ throughout $L$ trials is $\leq h^{-1}$ by definition of $L$.

nodes.name: Bound initial number of clauses
nodes.statement: The number of clauses with at most $k$ literals over $\{p_i, \bar{p}_i\}$ is less than $(2t)^{k+1}$.

nodes.name: Soundness: $g \Rightarrow f$ throughout
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be the product of all clauses $c$ of length $\leq k$ such that $f \Rightarrow c$. No clause of $B$ is ever deleted, hence $g \Rightarrow B$. Since $f$ is itself $k$-CNF, $B \equiv f$, so $g \Rightarrow f$ at every step.

nodes.name: Probabilistic guarantee via $L$
nodes.statement: Let $X = \sum_{v \Rightarrow f, v \not\Rightarrow g} D(v)$. Each EXAMPLES call has probability $X$ of triggering a deletion. Failure means $L = L(h,(2t)^{k+1})$ trials each succeed with probability $> h^{-1}$ but yield $< (2t)^{k+1}$ successes; this has probability $\leq h^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Theorem B: monotone DNF is learnable
nodes.statement: The class of monotone DNF expressions is learnable via an algorithm $B$ that uses $L = L(h,d)$ calls of EXAMPLES and $dt$ calls of ORACLE, where $d$ is the degree of the DNF expression $f$ to be learned and $t$ is the number of variables.
assumptions: $f$ is a monotone DNF expression of degree $d$ in $t$ variables
conclusions: $f$ is learnable using $L(h,d)$ EXAMPLES calls and $dt$ ORACLE calls

nodes.name: Algorithm B: Learn monotone DNF via EXAMPLES and ORACLE
nodes.statement: Maintain $g$ as a sum of monomials, initially $0$; on each example $v \not\Rightarrow g$, undetermine variables one by one (keeping ORACLE = 1) to obtain a prime implicant, and add it to $g$.
output: Monotone DNF expression $g$ that one-sidedly approximates $f$
nodes.pseudocode: g := 0; repeat L = L(h, d) times: v := EXAMPLES; if v ⊭ g then for i := 1 to t: let ṽ = v with p_i := *; if ORACLE(ṽ) = 1 then v := ṽ; let m = product of literals q with v ⊨ q; g := g + m.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem B
nodes.statement: Each iteration that fires adds a fresh prime implicant of $f$ (since the inner loop only undetermines variables when ORACLE remains 1), bounding ORACLE calls by $dt$. The remaining mass $X$ of $\{v : v \Rightarrow f, v \not\Rightarrow g\}$ either drops below $h^{-1}$ or the failure probability is $\leq h^{-1}$ by definition of $L(h,d)$.

nodes.name: Inner loop yields a prime implicant
nodes.statement: Starting from $v$ with $f(v)=1$, undetermining each $p_i$ that keeps ORACLE = 1 produces a vector $v$ whose conjunction $m$ of remaining literals is a prime implicant of $f$.

nodes.name: Distinct prime implicants bound ORACLE calls
nodes.statement: Each fired iteration adds a previously absent prime implicant, so the inner loop fires at most $d$ times, giving at most $dt$ ORACLE calls.

nodes.name: Probabilistic completion
nodes.statement: Let $X = \sum_{w \Rightarrow f, w \not\Rightarrow g} D(w)$; $X$ decreases monotonically. The probability $X$ never drops below $h^{-1}$ over $L(h,d)$ EXAMPLES calls is $\leq h^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Theorem B': DNF learnable on total-vector distributions
nodes.statement: If learnability is restricted to distributions $D$ with $D(v)=0$ whenever $v$ is not total, then the class of (unrestricted) DNF expressions is learnable; programs for the functions (not necessarily the concepts) can be deduced in $L(h,d)$ calls of EXAMPLES and $dt$ calls of ORACLE, where $d$ is the degree.
assumptions: $f$ is a DNF expression of degree $d$
conclusions: The function computed by $f$ is learnable using $L(h,d)$ EXAMPLES and $dt$ ORACLE calls

nodes.name: Open: monotone DNF from EXAMPLES alone
nodes.statement: Whether monotone DNF expressions can be learned from EXAMPLES alone (without ORACLE) is left open; a positive answer would be especially significant.

nodes.name: Learning monotone DNF from EXAMPLES alone
nodes.statement: Can the class of monotone DNF expressions be learned from EXAMPLES alone (no ORACLE calls)?

nodes.name: Bounded-disjunct DNF learnable from negative examples
nodes.statement: By dualizing Theorem A: for any $k$, the class of DNF expressions in which each disjunct has at most $k$ literals is learnable in polynomial time from negative examples alone (vectors $v$ with $\bar{f}(v) \neq 0$).
assumptions: each disjunct of $f$ has $\leq k$ literals
conclusions: $f$ is learnable in polynomial time using only negative examples

nodes.name: Theorem C: $\mu$-expressions are exactly learnable
nodes.statement: The class of $\mu$-expressions is learnable via a deduction procedure $C$ using $O(t^3)$ calls of $N$-ORACLE, $RP$, and $RA$ in total (and no calls of EXAMPLES). The procedure always deduces exactly the correct expression.
conclusions: $f$ is exactly identified by procedure $C$ in $O(t^3)$ oracle calls

nodes.name: Algorithm C: Learn $\mu$-expressions via N-ORACLE, RP, RA
nodes.statement: Identify the variables in $f$ via $RP(p_j)$, then alternately run plus-phases (group times-expressions by equivalence relation $S$ into sums) and times-phases (group plus-expressions by relation $T$ into products), each phase building one more level of the parse tree; auxiliary monomials $m_i, \tilde m_i$ are maintained via $PI$ and $RP$.
nodes.pseudocode: Initialize: for each p_j, if RP(p_j)=1 add single-variable expression g_j with m_j := p_j and tilde m_j computed by extending m via RP until PI(m m_j)=1. Repeat alternating phases: plus-phase computes equivalence S on times-expressions and forms new sums; times-phase computes equivalence T on plus-expressions and forms new products; update m_i, tilde m_i for each new/grafted g_i.

nodes.name: Claim 1: phase invariant on $g_i$
nodes.statement: After every phase, for every constructed $g_i$ there is exactly one subexpression $f_i$ of $f$ such that $g_i \preceq f_i$ and $f_i$ is of the same kind (plus or times) as $g_i$.

nodes.name: Claim 2: shared completion forces shared sum
nodes.statement: If $m_i, m_j$ are prime implicants of distinct times subexpressions $f_i, f_j$ of $f$ and there is some $m$ disjoint from both with $m_i m$ and $m_j m$ both prime implicants of $f$, then $f_i, f_j$ occur as summands of the same plus expression of $f$.

nodes.name: Claim 3: $S$ correctly groups times-expressions
nodes.statement: If Claim 1 holds and times-expressions $g_i, g_j$ have been formed with $g_i \preceq f_i$, $g_j \preceq f_j$ for times-expressions $f_i, f_j$, then $g_i, g_j$ are placed in the same sum at the next plus-phase iff $g_i = f_i$, $g_j = f_j$, and $f_i, f_j$ are addends in the same sum of $f$.

nodes.name: Claim 4: $T$ correctly groups plus-expressions
nodes.statement: If Claim 1 holds and plus-expressions $g_i \preceq f_i$, $g_j \preceq f_j$ have been found: (1) if $g_i = f_i$, $g_j = f_j$ and $f_i, f_j$ are multiplicands of the same times expression of $f$, then $g_i, g_j$ are placed in the same times expression at the next times-phase; (2) if $g_i, g_j$ ever land in the same times expression, then $f_i, f_j$ are in the same product in $f$.

nodes.name: Claim 5: depth-$k$ subexpressions found in $k$ phases
nodes.statement: If $f_i$ is a subexpression of $f$ of depth $k$, then after $k$ phases a $g_i$ identical to $f_i$ has been constructed.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem C
nodes.statement: Verify $S, T$ are equivalence relations using Claim 1; prove Claims 1, 3, 4 simultaneously by induction on phases; deduce by Claim 5 that every depth-$k$ subexpression of $f$ is recovered after $k$ phases. Total cost is dominated by computing $m_i, \tilde m_i$ ($O(t^3)$ N-ORACLE calls) and the equivalence $T$ ($O(t^3)$ RA calls).

nodes.name: $S$ and $T$ are equivalence relations
nodes.statement: Reflexivity and symmetry are immediate; transitivity of $T$ uses the definition of $RA$ directly, and transitivity of $S$ uses Claim 2.

nodes.name: Joint induction on Claims 1, 3, 4
nodes.statement: Induct on the number of phases; the simultaneous induction handles plus-phases via Claim 3 and times-phases via Claim 4 to maintain the phase invariant of Claim 1.

nodes.name: Depth completeness
nodes.statement: By Claim 5, every subexpression of depth $k$ is reconstructed exactly after $k$ phases, so after $\leq 2t-1$ phases the algorithm outputs $f$.

nodes.name: Runtime accounting
nodes.statement: Computing $m_i, \tilde m_i$ across the algorithm costs $O(t^2)$ PI calls i.e. $O(t^3)$ N-ORACLE calls; computing $T$ may ripple through up to $t$ sets, costing $O(t^3)$ RA calls.

nodes.name: Robots and elephants
nodes.statement: If a robot has a $k$-CNF recognition algorithm for elephants, Theorem A implies it can communicate the algorithm to other robots simply by exclaiming "elephant" whenever one appears (i.e., supplying positive examples).

nodes.name: Cryptographic obstruction to learning all polynomial circuits
nodes.statement: If there exist cryptographic functions $E_k$ that resist chosen-plaintext attack, then $E_k$ is not learnable; hence the conjectured existence of good easy-to-compute cryptographic functions implies that some easy-to-compute Boolean circuits are not learnable.

nodes.name: Variable count depends only on natural variables
nodes.statement: Using $L(h,|P|)$ EXAMPLES, one can approximate the set $P$ of variables ever determined in natural positive examples; consequently, learnability complexity may depend on $|P|$ rather than on the total universe size $t$.

nodes.name: Philosophical implications of learnability on natural inputs
nodes.statement: Since approximation only on natural inputs is required, learnable concepts are short programs distinguishing natural inputs; behavior on unnatural inputs is irrelevant, suggesting variability of meaning in distributed populations.

nodes.name: Tautology problem is co-NP-complete (Cook 1971)
nodes.statement: Determining whether a DNF formula is identically true is the tautology question of Cook, hence intractable in general.
nodes.origin_citation: Cook 1971, Complexity of theorem proving procedures

nodes.name: Chernoff tail bound for Bernoulli trials
nodes.statement: In $m$ independent trials each with success probability $\geq p$, the probability of at most $k$ successes (with $k < mp$) is at most $\binom{m}{k} p^k (1-p)^{m-k}$.
nodes.origin_citation: Chernoff (cf. Erdős-Spencer, Probabilistic Methods in Combinatorics)

nodes.name: Unrestricted Boolean circuits not learnable under factoring (Goldreich-Goldwasser-Micali)
nodes.statement: Under the hypothesis that integer factorization is intractable, the class of unrestricted Boolean circuits is not learnable from EXAMPLES and ORACLE restricted to total vectors.
